utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The next matter is this: that Judge Robinson is not able to be present, for urgent personal reasons which I hope have been conveyed to the parties. That being so, we cannot, of course, constituted as two Judges, make an order of the Trial Chamber. But what we propose to do is this: to hear submissions today, as it's convenient, the matter having been listed and the parties being before us, rather than putting matters off, to hear submissions today. Judge Robinson will, of course, have the transcript available to him and will participate in any of our decisions. Unless there's any objection, we propose to hear the submissions as we are presently constituted. Is there any objection from anybody?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: None, Sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCOURT
utterances.text: No objection, Sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Court has a request from the Defence for documentation, a total of 38 separate requests of a very sweeping nature. The ECMM have told us that they have an initial objection based upon Article 29 of the Statute and our powers to make the orders requested, and in those circumstances it may be convenient, Mr. McCourt, if you were to begin and set out the ground of your objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCOURT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before I set out those grounds, I should perhaps recall briefly the circumstances which resulted in ECMM making this appearance before the Tribunal this morning. On the 28th of December, 1999, ECMM received notice of the application before the Tribunal today. ECMM made contact with the senior legal officer of the Chamber to inform her that if instructed by the Portuguese head of the mission, who assumed responsibilities on the 1st of January of this year, that I would represent ECMM before this hearing. I would firstly like to apologise to the Tribunal for not having been in the position to notify the Tribunal in writing of my intention to appear or to submit in advance any written submissions. These were due to circumstances entirely outside of my own control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. McCourt, there is no need to apologise. We are grateful to you for being here on what's been fairly short notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCOURT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would also like to thank the Tribunal for having furnished me with a copy of the new Rule 54 bis. Next I would like to refer to the application for issuance of the order which was filed with the Tribunal, as I see, on the 1st of November, 1999. This application is made pursuant to Article 29(2) of the Statute of the Tribunal and Rule 54 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and ECMM wishes to object to the application on four separate grounds. The applicant has referred in his submission to the Tribunal to contacts made with ECMM on this issue, and I would like to inform the Tribunal of the full circumstances of those contacts before the application was made to this Tribunal. I would like to inform the Tribunal that it is correct that a Mr. Turner Smith, on behalf of the Defence, made a telephone call to my office in Sarajevo on the 13th of August, 1999. He informed me that he was representing Mr. Dario Kordic, and he asked for assistance of ECMM in a very general way. He sought access to ECMM records for the period 1991 to 1994 insofar as they relate to the Mostar actions, with a view to seeing if it was possible to find any documentation which might be useful to the Defence. I informed Mr. Turner Smith on the telephone that it was not possible for me to grant him the access which he had sought, and to the best of my recollection I also suggested that it would be appropriate for him to direct his request to the Office of the Prosecutor. On the 24th of August of last year, my office received a faxed letter from Mr. Turner Smith, a copy of which I propose to exhibit to the Tribunal. I think I have five copies there. Your Honours will see that in this letter, counsel sought an unspecified number of documents under some 15 separate headings. This list was quite a contrast from the nature of the initial request made by telephone to my office. In fact, this list is of such a general nature that it could involve reports from all over the ECMM mission area on a daily basis covering a period of some three and a half years. You will note that in that letter, on the last paragraph, counsel for the Defence also explained the reasons for his request, and you will note that he stated that he had reason to believe that many of the aforementioned materials may already be in the possession of the office of the Tribunal's Prosecutor. He went on to state that despite the obvious relevance of these materials to the matters at issue, as evidenced by the fact that the Prosecutor has herself introduced selected portions of these materials, he went on to say that the Prosecutor has refused to make full disclosure to the Defence. He went on to express the belief that the Prosecutor's position was not only contrary to both the letter and the spirit of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence, but that to the extent the Prosecutor has already introduced certain of these materials in the case, to withhold the balance of the materials violates the doctrine of completeness. He concluded by saying, "We are therefore obliged to seek to obtain these materials through whatever alternative avenues may be available to us." At the time this letter arrived in my office, I was away on business and also on some leave from my office in Sarajevo, and I returned there on the 10th of September. I replied to Mr. Turner Smith's letter by my letter of the 12th of September, and I would propose to exhibit -- I think I have already given the Court a copy of my reply letter as well. You will note that in my reply letter, I suggested that the Office of the Prosecutor, which had copied some of our archives, and that insofar as any of that material in its possession might be relevant to the case for the Defence, that that matter should be discussed with the Office of the Prosecutor. I also informed the Defence that any material copied to the Office of the Prosecutor from ECMM's archives was done so under the provisions of Rule 70 of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure. I also informed Mr. Turner Smith that I had advised the Office of the Prosecutor of his inquiry to my office and had requested the Office of the Prosecutor to deal directly with him and in consultation with ECMM. I did mention in my letter that ECMM was a European Union diplomatic mission, and that its archives are confidential, and that it wasn't possible for me to grant him the access he sought. I did, in fact, communicate with the Office of the Prosecutor, and I forwarded to his office a copy of the request from Mr. Turner Smith. I suggested to the Office of the Prosecutor that the matter would be best dealt with between the Office of the Prosecutor and the Defence directly, in consultation with ECMM. Since that time, ECMM has not had any further contact, either from counsel for Mr. Kordic or from The Office of the Prosecutor, about this matter until this date. Nothing further occurred with ECMM's involvement in this matter until I received the notification from the Tribunal of this hearing, which I said was on the 28th of December last. ECMM now proposes that the Tribunal should refuse to grant the order sought by the applicant on four specific grounds. The first ground are based on the fact that the application is made pursuant to Article 29(2) of the Statute of the Tribunal. This Article provides for co-operation by states with the Tribunal and, indeed, the provisions of Article 29 are limited to states. The term "state" is not defined in Article 29, nor, as far as I am aware, is it defined in the Statute itself. ECMM submits to the Tribunal that in those circumstances the normal rules of statutory interpretation apply, and that the term "state" must be given its normal, everyday meaning. In my submission to the Court, ECMM could not, under any of the normal meanings of the term "state," be considered to be a state. If one refers to the ordinary dictionary definition of "state," indeed even in the Concise Oxford Dictionary, it is defined as: "An organised political community under one government. A commonwealth, a nation, such a community forming part of a federal republic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCourt, I think there is no need to go into the details, because, after all, we do know what a state is. I think it will be more interesting for us if you could define for us what the ECMM is, because that is more interesting for us. We do know what a state is, we know what an international organisation is, and perhaps it might be of interest to us -- it would be of greater interest to us -- I don't know if you were able to hear me through the interpretation, so perhaps I could speak in English. [In English] It would be of greater interest for us to know what the ECMM is, because you spoke of a European mission. What is the exact legal status of the ECMM? And don't waste too much time on the concept of the state, because that could take us days and days, without actually achieving our end. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCOURT
utterances.text: The question of what exactly the legal status of ECMM is, is also, I submit to the Court, a rather difficult area of which -- which one could spend rather a lot of time discussing and debating. But, briefly, the ECMM mission was established by the member states of the European Community in 1991, as a result of an agreement concluded at Brioni on the 7th of July, 1991. As a result of this agreement, the European Community member states undertook to establish a monitor mission, initially for the purposes of monitoring Slovenia, to a certain extent Croatia, and with a liaison office in Belgrade. This agreement was formalised legally in the form of a memorandum of understanding signed in Belgrade on the 13th of July between the Yugoslav federal authorities, the separate republics, and also the -- on behalf of the member states of the European Community, 12 as they then were. There was, in fact, no decision by the European Community Council at the time in regard to the establishment of ECMM, nor was there a formal decision by the commission of the European Community in that regard. So, to answer your question, Your Honour, I would submit that ECMM can probably best be defined as being an ad hoc diplomatic mission mounted jointly by the member states of the European Union or, sorry, the European Community at that time. Since the implementation of the Amsterdam Treaty of last year, and the formalisation of the European Union itself, no decision has still been made on the legal status of ECMM. So it would be best to suggest that it is an ad hoc organisation, established for a specific purpose of monitoring in the region of the former Yugoslavia by the member states of the European Community, as it then was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's your first objection, Mr. McCourt, I take it, to do with Article 29?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCOURT
utterances.text: May it please your lordship, my first objection is that, under the provisions of Article 29, ECMM is not a state, and that therefore it would be inappropriate for the Tribunal to make such an order under the provisions of that Article. I would submit, accordingly, that the applicant has misdirected his application in applying it directly to ECMM under Article 29, and that ECMM is not a state, and that the Tribunal should refuse the application on that ground. That's my first ground of objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCourt, you said in the letter that you have submitted to us, I think, that you gave the documents to the Prosecutor, if I understand your letter correctly -- to the Office of the Prosecutor -- invoking Article 70 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCOURT
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I read that somewhere. It's in your letter dated the 12th of September, addressed to Mr. Turner. [In English] "Advise you that The Office of the Prosecutor has provided some of our archives and that insofar as any of the material in its possession might be relevant to your case, you should discuss your request with that office. I should also inform you that any material provided by the Office of the Prosecutor from archives was done so under the provisions of Rule 70 of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure." [Interpretation] What do you mean, that this was done under the provisions of Article 70? Could you tell us, please, what you meant by saying this in your letter?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCOURT
utterances.text: Your Honour, by referring to Article 70, this is an agreement that was reached before my time in ECMM, between The Office of the Prosecutor and ECMM, I think in 1996, whereby access, not unlimited access, but access to the archives of ECMM was granted to The Office of the Prosecutor. The office was permitted to copy the archives, but those copies were subject to the matters not subject to disclosure under the provisions of Rule 70 of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence. By this it was intended that if The Office of the Prosecutor wished to proceed and use any of those materials in its Prosecution of cases, that it would be necessary for the Tribunal to consult with ECMM again about the specific documents it proposed to use, and that ECMM would consider whether it had any further objections to such documents being put in evidence, and if not, the Tribunal would be forwarded the -- rather, I should say, that the Prosecutor would be authorised to use those documents for the purpose of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, there was an agreement between The Office of the Prosecutor and the ECMM. As far as I understood, the ECMM is, in fact, the European Community. It doesn't have legal personality as such. And when we address the ECMM, we are actually addressing the European Community, which has since become the European Union. And you yourself, in order to come here, you asked for authorisation from the current presidency of the European Union, which is held by Portugal, to come here. So you are part of the European Union, which is a regional organisation, not in the sense of the charter, but it is an organisation of a regional nature. Therefore, there was an agreement between you yourselves and the Prosecutor in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCOURT
utterances.text: Your Honour, the position is that, as I understand it, a legal distinction must be drawn between the European Community's Monitor Mission established and run by the member states, in particular by the member state which is holding the presidency for the time being of the European Union, and that a legal distinction must be drawn between that organisation and the European Community itself, and also between the European Union and the Monitoring Mission, that these are, as I understand it, separate entities in law, and that the basis for the establishment of ECMM is not that it is an official organ of the European Community as such, but that it was an ad hoc agreement put together in 1991 by the member states. If it were an EU organisation, one would expect it to be funded and staffed by the European Union itself. The reality is otherwise. The head of the mission is appointed by the country which holds the presidency for the time being, and at this time that is a Portuguese ambassador. The staffing of the Monitor Mission is provided by the member states directly. Each monitor is appointed by his own government, and the costs associated with that are borne by the member state sending the monitor. So the European Union doesn't fund, finance, or manage the organisation itself. This may, of course, change in the future, but for the time being that is the present arrangement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, if I follow you well -- that is why you are here, anyway, to provide some clarification -- the ECMM was founded by an agreement -- I wouldn't call it an ad hoc agreement. It's just an agreement -- in 1991 between the European states, who were members of the European Union at the time. Could you provide us with a copy of that agreement from 1991 for the Court, established by the European Union, as well as the agreement on cooperation with the countries in the region that you just referred to that followed the agreement of 1991? So we would need the documents that you have mentioned for the needs of this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCOURT
utterances.text: If it please the Court, I propose to exhibit a copy of the relevant memorandum of understanding in respect of the Mission's activities in Bosnia-Herzegovina associated with my second objection to the granting of the order sought by the applicant in this case. I should, of course, refer back to what Your Honour has said about the European Union in 1991, and of course there wasn't such an entity at that time. There was the European Community, which is legally separate and distinct from the European Union, which came into effect, as I understand it, with the Amsterdam Treaty, and the legal distinction must continue to be drawn between the two. As regards the agreement in 1991 to establish the Mission, there was no signed agreement, as such, by the member states. The only document upon which the existence of the Mission was based at the time was the memorandum of understanding with the host parties in the region. That was signed on behalf of the member states by a representative of the country which held the presidency at that time. I can produce to the Court a copy of not the initial memorandum of understanding, which didn't involve Bosnia at all, but to recap briefly on the circumstances at the time, the Mission was initially established to deal primarily with Slovenia, as I said, and that was the first memorandum of understanding. That particular crisis was resolved rather quickly, as you will recall. However, the situation in Croatia deteriorated, and there was a second memorandum of understanding signed to expand the Mission's activities into Croatia. This memorandum was signed on the 1st of September, 1991. A third memorandum of understanding was signed on the 1st of October, 1991, to establish the Mission's activities in what was then the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina within the region. That is now, of course, Bosnia and Herzegovina since the Dayton Agreement times, and I would submit that in the context of the Defence application in respect of documents relating to the Bosnia and Herzegovina area, the relevant MOU, or memorandum of understanding, is that which was signed on the 1st of October, 1991, and I propose to exhibit to the Court a copy of that memorandum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Mr. McCourt. But if you have a copy of the agreement which you shared with the Prosecutor, it would be welcome by the Chamber if we could have a copy of that document as well, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCOURT
utterances.text: If it please Your Honour, I'm not in a position to produce to the Tribunal a copy of that particular one at this time. I don't have it with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but you could have it sent to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCOURT
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I will do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, in fact, there was an agreement with the Prosecutor, with the Office of the Prosecutor, and that is how you invoked Rule 70. Did you not plan to have the same agreement with the Defence as the one you had with the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCOURT
utterances.text: Your Honour, no agreement has been concluded with any party, other than the Office of the Prosecutor, in regard to access to ECMM's archives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I'm asking, Mr. McCourt, is whether you could not envisage to enter into consultation with the Defence, too, to see to what extent you may be able to provide access to them to exculpatory documents, documents which, of course, they would need to specify. Could you envisage providing access to the Defence, in the same way that you have done for the Office of the Prosecutor, without going into an order to be addressed to you? Because it is not necessary to issue such an order if you simply enter into an agreement with the Defence to see to what extent the Defence may have access to some exculpatory documents which are in the possession of the ECMM.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCOURT
utterances.text: Your Honour, in that regard ECMM has not, to date, been prepared to grant access to its archives to anybody other than the Office of the Prosecutor. But I will deal with the matters which you have referred to in other aspects of the submission which I would wish to make to the Tribunal, and I would submit that there is another way of dealing with it which would be more appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Can we move to your second objection, which was based on the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCOURT
utterances.text: Your Honour, my second ground for asking the Tribunal to refuse the application relates to the status of the records themselves which are involved. As I've said, ECMM was established in July 1991, after the agreement in Brioni on the 7th of July of that year. The legal basis for the Mission rests on a number of memorandums of understanding which were subsequently signed, and as I said, the relevant one for the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as it then was, was that which was signed on the 1st of October, 1991, a copy of which I have now exhibited to the Tribunal. I should apologise for the quality of the copy, but it's the best I could do in the field with what was available to me. I would like to refer to the preambler [phoen] paragraphs which set out the context in which ECMM was established in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Court will see that there was a decision of the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe initially, which welcomed the readiness of the European Community and its member states to organise the Mission.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you slow down, please, for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCOURT
utterances.text: You will see also a reference to the invitation by the Yugoslav authorities to the European Community and its member states to organise such a mission. You will note a reference to the agreements reached at Brioni on the 7th of July, '91, and you will also note the conclusion of a memorandum of understanding in Belgrade on the 13th of July, '91, and the further memorandum of understanding of the 1st of September, '91. You will also note that the member states of the European Community, as it then was, 12 in all, are specifically named as being sending parties. Article 1 of this memorandum of understanding refers to the mandate of the Mission in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Article 4 deals with status, and Article 4(2) makes a provision for unrestricted freedom of movement. Article 5 provides for the composition of the Mission; personnel would be appointed by the sending parties; that such personnel belonging to the Monitor Mission will be called monitors and that they will be appointed by the governments of the monitoring parties. You will see that there is a provision for the members of the Mission's administrative and technical staff enjoying a status similar to that of administrative and technical staff from monitoring parties employed in embassies, and a similar provision in respect of the Mission's auxiliary personnel. If I can move on to Article 10, you will see that monitors will be granted, during their mission, the privileges and immunities of diplomatic agents in accordance with the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, and that these privileges and immunities will be granted during their mission and thereafter with respect to acts performed during the mission. You will see that the memorandum of understanding is drafted in a way to make provision for the Mission to be a diplomatic mission in all respects, with the provisions of the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations applying to the Mission. In that regard, I would like to make a reference to the provisions of the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, and I have, for the Tribunal's convenience, copies of the Vienna Convention which I propose to refer to. Before doing so, it's quite clear -- I think it should be to the Tribunal -- that the Mission and its members, its premises, and its activities have been accorded the status of a diplomatic mission. There is also a provision that the premises of the Mission are inviolable. Therefore, it is, I submit, clear that the Mission has diplomatic status in accordance with the terms of the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations of 1961. A diplomatic agent is defined in the Vienna Convention, on the first page, as the head of the Mission or a member of the diplomatic staff of the Mission. Article 22 of the Convention provides that the premises of the Mission shall be inviolable and also that the premises of the Mission, their furnishings and other property thereon, and the means of transport of the Mission shall be immune from search, requisition, attachment, or execution. I want to make a particular reference to Article 24, which states that the archives and documents of the Mission shall be inviolable at any time and wherever they may be. Now, the original of this Convention is, as I understand it, deposited with the Secretary-General of the United Nations. I should say that the ECMM mission is headed by a Portuguese diplomatic who is designated ambassador while holding that appointment. Furthermore, in Bosnia and Herzegovina all monitors are registered as diplomatic representatives with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and issued with diplomatic ID cards. The Mission is accepted as a diplomatic mission by all of the host countries where it operates. Furthermore, ECMM's vehicles are exempt from registration and licensing requirements and carry CD markings. ECMM is claiming before this Tribunal the diplomatic privileges which attach to its archives under the provisions of the memorandum of understanding and the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations. In my respectful submission to the Tribunal, it is clear that the records of ECMM are protected by those privileges which are provided by both the MOU, memorandum of understanding, and the Vienna Convention, and that accordingly they are not subject to an order for disclosure from any court, either national or international, including, in this case, in my respectful submission, this Tribunal. I therefore submit that this Tribunal should refuse the application on the grounds -- this additional ground of the status of the Mission. This, of course, does not preclude the ECMM from assisting the Tribunal by voluntary disclosure of records to the Office of the Prosecutor and by the arrangements it has or is prepared to agree with the Office of the Prosecutor regarding disclosure to the Defence in the interests of justice, and this brings me, if I may, to my third ground of objection to the granting of the order sought by the Defence. ECMM has, as I've said, agreed to co-operate with the Office of the Prosecutor in the important work which it is doing. I should emphasise, however, that ECMM does not have any investigative function in the context of the role of the Office of the Prosecutor. Under the provisions of Rule 70 of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence, ECMM has provided access to ICTY to its archives. This access is not unrestricted, as has been suggested by the applicant. As I've said, it means that ECMM must further authorise the use of any of its records for the purposes of the Office of the Prosecutor on a case-by-case and document-by-document basis. To date, to the best of my knowledge, ECMM has agreed to any such requests from the Office of the Prosecutor. In the context of the applicant's statement in his letter of the 24th of August to ECMM, when he spoke about the refusal of the Prosecution to make full disclosure, it seems logical to me that an application for discovery might more appropriately have been lodged by the Defence against the Office of the Prosecutor rather than ECMM, if that hasn't already been done. And as I understand it, there is provision for such an application under Subrule 66(B) of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence. It may, of course, be the case that that would have produced a reciprocal requirement on the Defence to disclose matters it would prefer not to to the Prosecutor, but so be it. It would appear, therefore, to ECMM, that it would have been much more appropriate for the Defence to have dealt with his requirements on this basis. Therefore, ECMM submits that the Tribunal should not make the order sought, on the additional grounds that such an order is not required in the interests of justice, when an acceptable alternative procedure is already available under the provisions of Rule 66(B). I should say, in that regard, that ECMM would be prepared to very seriously consider any request from the Office of the Prosecutor, where the Prosecutor considered that disclosure of information in its possession would be warranted to the Defence under the provisions of Rule 68 of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure. Again, of course, this would be on a document-by-document basis. ECMM, therefore, submits that the Court should refuse the application on this additional ground, because it is not necessary in the interests of justice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCourt, you certainly know that The Office of the Prosecutor need not share the interests and concerns of the Defence. You are quoting our Rules and you must be familiar with the Statute and the Rules of Procedure of the Tribunal. And there are two parties: There is the Prosecutor and there is the Defence. And to refer the Defence to the Prosecution, it is difficult to do, because the Defence, of course, is the adversary party, the opposing party, and it is quite possible that by referring them to The Office of the Prosecutor, it cannot really quite meet all their concerns, and I do not really think that it would meet the objectives of the Defence. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCOURT
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may refer to Rule 68. And of course I fully understand the point that Your Honour has made. But the Prosecutor has a duty of disclosure under the provisions of Rule 68, and this is a duty which The Office of the Prosecutor must obviously comply with under the specific Rules --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but, Mr. McCourt, it is bound to disclose, it is under the obligation to show or give the documents that it has. But it is quite possible that there are other documents which it has not requested and which are yet of interest to the Defence. The Rule, the obligation [indiscernible] is to operate. The Chamber is already taking care of this and, for your information, we have already requested the Prosecution to give all that it has in the nature of exculpatory documents to the Defence. But the problem is, the question that arises is whether there are some other documents which the Prosecution has not requested and which are in your possession and which could be of interest to the Defence. So are you refusing to do that, and are you refusing to discuss it with Defence, or are you still leaving some room for possible discussion of such documents for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCOURT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I have stated ECMM's position with regard to the status of its documents, and ECMM would have a serious difficulty in changing its position in regard to the status, the confidential nature of its diplomatic archives. In accordance with the provisions of Article 24 of the Vienna Convention, these documents are confidential and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They are confidential, all the documents are confidential, in view of the convention on documents, but this is not a matter that concerns the Tribunal in this -- the problem is that this -- that when you placed some documents on the Prosecution, you did not raise this objection. You did not say that they were confidential. You agreed to give those documents, to disclose those documents to the Prosecution. Now, why are you raising this objection now, when it comes to a Defence? There is a problem, I believe, here of -- the problem of equity, of fairness which arises, because we are dealing here with International Tribunal. There are accused persons who risk to be detained, have been here for a long time, and, presumably, everybody should have access to documents, both inculpatory and exculpatory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCOURT
utterances.text: Your Honour, my instructions are that these documents should not be made available to anybody other than The Office of the Prosecutor for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCourt, let's just consider that for a moment. The argument is that the documents are inviolable. This is leaving aside your objections under Article 29. But that can't be right, if you've agreed to give them to the Prosecutor. What, perhaps, we might have some difficulty in understanding, is how it comes about that they are not inviolable when it comes to the Prosecutor, but they are inviolable when it comes to the Defence. There may not be a consistency here which is apparent. Now, of course, you may well say that with regard to the Prosecutor, you have the assurances under Rule 70 of confidentiality, which are otherwise missing. But if there were similar assurances under Rule 70 obtained by the Court from the Defence, would the objections still arise, providing, of course, the other criteria are established under the Blaskic judgement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCOURT
utterances.text: Your Honour, the position of ECMM in this matter would be, and is, that it had no difficulty in granting access to its archives under Rule 70 to The Office of the Prosecutor. The Mission was quite prepared to do that, in the knowledge that the documentation would be well and truly protected and that any subsequent use would require further consultation with ECMM. ECMM's view on advancing that disclosure beyond that office would be that it's not necessary to go any further than that; that since The Office of the Prosecutor is fully aware and conscious, I'm sure fully complies with its obligations under the Rules of Procedure, including those of Rule 68, that it would be for the Office of the Prosecutor to analyse those records and to make a judgement on what documents might indeed be exculpatory. The Office of the Prosecutor has the knowledge and the skills relating to such matters which ECMM doesn't have, and, of course, the access that was granted to the Office of the Prosecutor was done so in the belief that it would be sufficient to meet with the requirements of justice, not only to the Prosecutor but indeed to the Defence as well, and that the responsibility for deciding on what might be useful to the Defence should properly rest, indeed in this case, with the Prosecution, rather than with ECMM as an organisation, which doesn't involve itself in making any such determinations as to relevance of its records.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I mean, clearly not. You wouldn't be in a position to do that. The difficulty, as Judge Bennouna has pointed out, with that position is that that requires one side to establish what is significant and important to the other. Now, the Rules do that, of course, as far as the material in the possession of the Prosecutor is concerned, but there may be material which -- the relevance of which and the importance of which is clear only to one party in the litigation. It isn't necessarily clear to the other. But shall we -- I think we've debated that far enough. Shall we move on to your fourth objection, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCOURT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. ECMM's fourth ground for opposing this application is that although ECMM is not, in our submission, a state, and therefore an order shouldn't be granted under Article 29, but even if it were, ECMM submits that the applicant has not properly complied with the terms of the new Rule 54 bis. The application now before the Court contains an annex listing materials sought from ECMM under some 38 headings. ECMM recalls the initial oral request of the 13th of August, 1999 was completely unspecific and was of a very general nature. Total records over a period of some three and a half years relating to the Mostar region is what was initially sought, with a view to finding out if there was anything that might be useful to the Defence. The subsequent written request, which had been -- which I have a copy of -- has been produced to the Tribunal, dated the 24th of August, 1999, relates to an unspecified number of documents under some 15 headings. Now, in its application before the Court, in the annex attached to it, the applicant has added additional material, which was never in fact requested from ECMM, and perhaps not from The Office of the Prosecutor either. But it has also dropped some of the informations previously requested. The application now is not for a specific number of clearly identified documents. The applicant has, in my respectful submission, fairly to indicate adequately how the documents sought might be relevant and necessary for its case. And since many of these documents were never requested from ECMM, it is clear that the applicant had not explained what steps had previously been taken to secure them from The Office of the Prosecutor within the provisions of the Rules. The access now sought by the applicant, to practically all of ECMM's records, for a considerable period, could also prejudice the security of ECMM's interlocutors in the Mission area and, indeed, perhaps also its own staff. I should say that in the time available before this hearing, it was not feasible or practicable to consider the full extent of the security considerations which would have to be evaluated on a document-by-document basis. Accordingly, it was not possible to submit to the Tribunal the notice of objection, which is required under the provisions of Subrule 54 bis (F), before this hearing took place, other than to make this general oral submission in that regard. I therefore respectfully seek the Tribunal's indulgence and understanding of ECMM's position in that regard. I should say that the task of considering each and every one of the documents, comprehended by the applicant's request under some 38 headings, would be enormous. It could involve many, many hundreds of documents and would be extremely and unduly onerous to the organisation. ECMM is not staffed for these purposes. The applicant has also referred to four requirements for the issue of a binding order under Article 29(ii), and claims to have complied with each of the four such requirements. If those four requirements are correctly articulated in the application, and ECMM is not in a position to dispute that, ECMM's reply would be as follows: A, the documents requested under many headings are in broad categories rather than specific documents; B, the relevance and necessity of the documents to the Defence in this case has not been adequately established; C, the applicant has sought at least hundreds, if not perhaps even thousands of documents, which is not permitted by the Rules. And as I've already said, their production would be extremely onerous and overly taxing, under very limited resources of ECMM. In that regard, I should say to the Tribunal, ECMM has one part-time databank attendant and has no archivist. The time required by ECMM to provide the materials sought would be very considerably in excess of the 60 days suggested in the application. I couldn't hazard a guess as to how long it would take. Accordingly, while ECMM submits that the Tribunal should refuse the order under the three previous arguments submitted, ECMM also submits that the Tribunal should reject this application on the grounds that the applicant has not fully complied with the provisions of Rule 54 bis. What I have said to date relates only to the application on behalf of Mr. Kordic. In the case of the application joinder by Mr. Cerkez, if I pronounce the gentleman's name correctly, ECMM has, of course, never had any contact whatsoever on his behalf, either orally or in writing. No request at all has been received on his behalf. Accordingly, in respect of his joinder in this application, ECMM respectfully submits that his application should also be refused by the Tribunal for the same reasons. In conclusion, ECMM submits that the application on behalf of both the Defence should be refused by this Tribunal. I thank you gentlemen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCourt. Mr. Stein, we are going to hear the arguments now. I'm afraid the clock is not with you. We have what is in the application. There is no need to repeat that. I think we have in mind your probable arguments in relation to relevance, which we've, with respect, heard before.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: I'll try to be the taciturn Yankee. May it please the Court, first, with regard to the states issue raised by the ECMM, the very documents that the ECMM provides are documents between the states. This is exactly, almost a shell between the Netherlands who was here this morning and said, "We are a state, but we gave our documents to UNPROFOR. Get them from them." The Netherlands, as part of this group, the logic of what we are hearing before Your Honours, totally, is these documents are unavailable to all. We suggest that ECMM does come within 29(ii), because it's composed of member states of the U.N., and that the present application should be viewed as an application to those member states. Even if Your Honours disagree with that, then we suggest that the Chamber has within its power the appropriate -- and it would be an appropriate exercise of Your Honours' power to order a subpoena to the ECMM pursuant to Article 15 and Rule 54. With regard to prior discussions and attempts to get documents through conciliatory means, cutting to the chase and being as succinct as I can, it doesn't matter what we would have done, could have done, might have done, or ought to have done; their answer was clear and unequivocal, as expressed in the letter and in the submissions today. Their files are privileged. They are confidential, except when they are not confidential, which is when the Prosecution is given access. Third, with regard to that very issue, having waived the confidentiality that they now assert, by giving the documents to the Prosecutor, we will be in the anomalous position again of having the Prosecution using the various documents that have been given to it, relying on it, relying on witnesses from the ECMM, but us having no access to them. And we may be in a situation where ultimately we might move to strike the testimony or exhibits, the documentary evidence of the Prosecution submitted by the ECMM for one side of the case, but not to the other. I hope we don't have to go there. I would point out that Your Honour Judge Bennouna exactly has the point that we make. Our view of the case is very different from the Prosecutor's. Our eyes looking at the documents are very different than the Prosecution. Although I do quote to Your Honours, Mr. Nice's observation at one point, and this would be on day 71, "I thought that the ECMM documents generally are documents that both sides are going to regard as helpful when they are produced." And you will recall the testimony of Mr. Brix-Andersen on day 95, November 30th. This is from line 20. "So my knowledge of him is from the documents, from the reports, namely, from RC Zenica. Based on these reports, it was the assessment of the ECMM and my own opinion that Mr. Kordic had an influential position, in some areas a controlling position, within the HVO." So the Prosecution has been using the documents, and the witnesses for the Prosecution have been using the documents, and we believe under equality of arms we are entitled to them. And I will try to change the word "arms" henceforth. Finally, we want to narrow our request. I took a look at this with my colleagues last night, and so we would limit our request, if I may, Your Honour, to that set out at paragraphs 3, 6, 10, 12 through 15 inclusive, 18, 21 through 31 inclusive, and 38. The others we find over-broad, and I don't want to get into an issue of that magnitude. I promised I would be succinct. I didn't even think I would do it in six minutes, but I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just add one simple statement? We did join with the formal submission to the request of the Kordic Defence. The idea was really based on the principle of beneficium corisiones [phoen]. And in the same time, since we are obliged by the earlier orders of that Court related to the confidentiality of the documents, we believe that all the documents we might possibly get, based on the Kordic Defence request -- better to say order which you may or may not issue -- we will benefit from that. We don't think that there is any formal obstacle in our omitting requesting the document from the involved parties, since the other Defence did it. Thank you, Sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I might want to add -- I'm sorry, I forgot one thing. The gentleman from the ECMM might want to check the record and with the Office of the Prosecutor. There have been documents from the ECMM entered, I believe. I believe Z2451.6 is one such document. I don't believe there has been any application made to the ECMM for some sort of waiver of confidentiality, so I think that the door is not only open, but wide open. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll consider these matters and give our order in due course when Judge Robinson has returned, which will be after the 25th of this month. As I say, we're grateful to Mr. McCourt for attending to assist the Tribunal. I don't want to break for the moment, but there is the UNPROFOR matter. We've got the response on that. Is there anything you want to say about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: No, except that I believe, literally read, we couldn't share the information with the defendant. The restrictions that UNPROFOR wants are acceptable to us in terms of confidentiality. They talk about the lawyers for Mr. Kordic having access to the information. They neglect "the defendant." I'm sure that's an oversight.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: And we're working with the UNPROFOR officials as we speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A final question, Mr. Stein. I think that this applies -- excuse me for a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Concerning your request for documents to the Netherlands as a state, it was stated this morning that a certain number of documents concerning the chain of command, or the Dutch army, or certain units of that army, that those documents should be requested from UNPROFOR rather than the Netherlands as, in the opinion of the Netherlands, it does not have the possibility or the right to communicate them because that is up to the United Nations. For this type of documents for which it has been established that the only way that they can be disclosed is through the United Nations and UNPROFOR, could you address yourself to UNPROFOR rather than the Netherlands, therefore to change, in a sense, the addressee, the person to whom your request is addressed?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Of course we can, Your Honour. Frankly, the biggest dilemma we have with UNPROFOR is its over-willingness. They have 4.000 boxes of documents, so we have to find the Netherlands in that 4.000 boxes. We can do it and we will do it, and, if necessary, if that's all we have, that's all we have. On the other hand, the discrete state, if it had its own discrete records, would have made our task far easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now until Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: concluded at 1.13 p.m.
